61a80ce108: FarmPartner is an AI engine that helps farmers adapt to climate change and make better decisions about their land, starting with crop rotation. It cross-references NASA Earth observation data, information about each farm and the practical knowledge of experienced farmers, and delivers personalized recommendations through a chatbot on the messaging apps farmers already use. It is built for generational renewal, passing that know-how on to the next generation of farmers; for digital inclusion, since anyone can use it by voice or by text; and with no language barriers, in 46 languages.

4fd3aad4a1: Intensive farming wears out the land
26d3077d4f: Planting the same crop year after year exhausts the soil: it loses nutrients and organic matter, pests and erosion increase, and every season yields less. Crop rotation is essential to let the land recover, but choosing the right rotation means knowing each field’s climate, soil and water.
30b5df74f6: The climate is changing faster than experience
c8b0bce86c: Rain, frost and heat waves no longer follow the usual calendar. What worked for decades is no longer reliable.
4d97903d46: The data exists, but it doesn’t reach the field
45363f0868: NASA has been observing every plot on the planet for more than 20 years. But that data comes in technical formats, in English, and is made for scientists.
8d35d90442: Many experienced farmers retire with no one to take over, and what they know is never written down.
35ec3987f1: Farming tools are often complex apps, in a single language, that require reading charts or being comfortable with technology.

58d4555017: Honest advice starts with being honest about its own gaps. These are the known limits of the current version of FarmPartner. The bot says them out loud in its answers too, so every farmer knows how far to trust each recommendation.
4adf6c158d: Crop rules are a first approximation.
e5d124edd7: Crop traits and scoring weights are hackathon approximations from public extension guidance. They need agronomist review. New combinations from the rotation search are less proven: try them on part of a field first.
c35c44f909: How much heat, water or frost each crop tolerates, and how much each factor weighs in the score, comes from general public guidance, not from a study of your region.
d117499f74: Use the scores to compare options and start a conversation, not as a final verdict. If something doesn’t match your experience, trust your experience and tell the bot.
fc7afbb156: Review by agronomists, validation with farmers in real fields, and the know-how of experienced farmers feeding the knowledge base the AI consults.
d84e40514f: Satellites see in blocks, not in fields.
5b8a3acf96: POWER is a ~50 km model grid, and a MODIS pixel (250 m) can mix fields. CDL can mislabel some years. GRACE is a ~300 km signal: the regional aquifer trend, not one well.
4bcffb922d: NASA POWER climate describes a square about 50 km wide. One MODIS vegetation pixel covers 250 × 250 m, so a small or narrow field can be blended with its neighbors. The USDA crop map (CDL) is itself made from satellites and sometimes gets a year wrong. GRACE groundwater trends describe a region about 300 km across.
40faa08ba3: Climate reads describe your area rather than your exact plot. Microclimates such as valleys, slopes or frost pockets may not show. If the crop history looks wrong, correct it in the chat.
a7c66e9fba: Finer-resolution sources such as Landsat (30 m) for vegetation, plus the farmer’s own corrections, which always take priority over the satellite reading.
39197c38e4: No local prices yet. “Income” is a relative index plus the trial-based yield effect, and the bot asks farmers for local prices and buyers.
6f2607b385: FarmPartner doesn’t know your market prices or your own yields. The “income” score ranks rotations against each other, using a relative market index and the yield gain that 3,663 field trials show after each previous crop (Mudare et al. 2025); it is not a forecast in dollars or euros.
965d927293: Before switching crops, check local prices, buyers and contracts. The bot asks you about them so the comparison reflects your real market.
36db4f3cb3: Connecting local price and yield data, and learning from the prices and buyers farmers share in the conversation.
6190994efb: Deepest in the U.S., useful worldwide.
42bb041cab: U.S.-deepest: CDL and SSURGO are U.S.-only. Climate, NDVI and the forecast work worldwide; outside the U.S. the farmer types their crops and FAOSTAT limits the search to crops the country grows.
ed9c78a361: Crop history (USDA CDL) and detailed soil data (USDA SSURGO) only exist for the United States. NASA climate, vegetation health (NDVI), soil moisture, crop stress, groundwater trends and the weather forecast cover the whole planet.
cab498de16: Outside the U.S., tell the bot which crops you grow and what your soil is like. The climate analysis works just the same; crop history and soil detail come from you.
ad0a235cf9: Global soil and crop-type datasets, so farmers everywhere get the same depth of analysis without typing it in.
b13fdefd46: Some satellites answer minutes later, and not every day.
e4d8bc4f0e: SMAP is a 9 km grid. ECOSTRESS passes are irregular, and clouds leave gaps. Both arrive 20–30 minutes after onboarding, and until then the report lists them as “processing”.
7d1812bc46: SMAP (soil moisture) and ECOSTRESS (crop water stress) are requested from NASA AppEEARS for each new field. NASA processes them as a queue, so they come in 20–30 minutes after the first answer. SMAP describes a 9 km square; ECOSTRESS sees 70 m but only on the days the space station passes over, and clouds hide some of those passes.
6a9b1d99b2: Your first comparison uses climate, vegetation and crop maps; soil moisture and crop stress are added to the report and to the watering advice once they arrive. If your soil is wetter or drier than the bot thinks, say so.
69eab23454: Requesting the satellite data ahead of time for common farming regions, and adding finer, more frequent soil-moisture products as they become available.
abefcd8ea6: A recommendation is only useful if you know how far to trust it. That’s why every answer comes with its evidence, the data gaps and the risks to check locally.

d85f0cd168: FarmPartner needs to know where your field is to read it from space, and your number to reply to you. Here is exactly what we keep, who sees what, and how to make it go away.
83b2504bfa: We never sell, rent or share your phone number. It is used only to reply to you on WhatsApp or SMS, and it is never sent to the AI, to NASA or to any data service.
0c17998ea1: To fetch satellite and weather data we send only the field’s coordinates to public services (NASA, USDA, Open‑Meteo). They never receive your number, your name or anything else that identifies you.
8c5e8e359b: The AI never sees who you are
b64abb2136: Claude, the AI behind the advice, gets your messages and your field’s data, labelled with the county or town — not your phone number.
c2940b261f: Each field report lives at a random, unguessable address. It shows the area and the analysis — never your number or your name.
8eea2a1f5d: We don’t show ads and we don’t sell data. What you tell us about your field is used to give you better advice, and nothing else.
02beeaa484: Text STOP and we won’t message you first again. Text RESET to erase your fields. Write to us and we’ll delete everything.
05d89a8795: Every outside service FarmPartner talks to, and what it receives.
44b8ce9bf7: Your messages and photos, your field’s area and data
a9997b86c4: Voice notes, to turn them into text and back
a22d0a88d8: Your number and our replies — they carry the messages
c9d5af7231: ✕ Your field data beyond the replies themselves
38647954c9: The fine print, still in plain words
70c28593e5: Your phone number, language, your field’s location and crops, your goals, the conversation, and anything you report (rain, pests, yields). We keep them together so the bot remembers your field next time you write.
5e82a4e1c6: Raw satellite images. We store only the summaries computed for your field (rainfall, soil, vegetation trends), not the original NASA files.
0096b8dd2c: In a private Postgres database (Supabase) that only the FarmPartner server, which runs on Google Cloud in Europe, can read. Public access to its tables is switched off.
bb2a16f7cc: Text RESET to remove your fields and their history. To erase your number and conversation as well, e‑mail hello@farmpartner.space from anywhere, with the number you used.
